mercy_translation.text:
Perhaps you wonder why, when we have set out to speak about the Word’s becoming man, we are now telling the story of the beginning of humanity. Yet this too is not foreign to the purpose of our account.

For when speaking of the Savior’s manifestation among us, we must also speak about the origin of human beings, so that you may know that our condition became the occasion of his descent, and that our transgression called forth the Word’s loving-kindness, so that the Lord came even to us and appeared among human beings.

We became the occasion of his embodiment; and for the sake of our salvation he acted in loving-kindness so as to come to be and appear in a human body.

Thus God made the human being and willed that he remain in incorruption. But human beings, becoming careless and turning away from the contemplation of God, devising and imagining evil for themselves—as was said earlier—came under the condemnation of death that had been threatened beforehand. They no longer remained as they had been made; rather, according to what they had chosen, they were being corrupted, and death held royal sway over them. For transgression of the commandment returned them to what belongs to them by nature, so that just as they had come into being from non-being, so in time they might naturally undergo corruption toward non-being.

For if, having once possessed by nature no existence at all, they were called into being by the presence and loving-kindness of the Word, then it followed that, once human beings had emptied themselves of the knowledge of God and turned toward things that are not—for evil things are not truly beings, while good things are, since they have come from the God who is—it followed that they would also be emptied of continued existence. This is what it means to be dissolved and remain in death and corruption.

For by nature the human being is mortal, since he came into being from non-being. Yet because of his likeness to the One who is, had he preserved that likeness through contemplation of him, he would have blunted his natural corruption and remained incorruptible. As Wisdom says, “Attention to the laws is the confirmation of incorruption.” And being incorruptible, he would thereafter have lived as God, as divine Scripture also indicates somewhere when it says, “I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you die like human beings and fall like one of the rulers.”

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius distinguishes created mortality from the gift of incorruption sustained by participation in and contemplation of God.
The statement that humanity might 'live as God' belongs to Athanasius' theology of participation and does not erase the Creator-creature distinction.
